transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-27 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Kapoor (AtlasPulse Head of Platform), Maya Lin (AtlasPulse Cloud Architect), Ethan Brooks (AtlasPulse Product)
Link references: packaging checklist (internal GH), draft SOW (drive link), sample telemetry schema (doc link)

[00:00] Sofia M: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick round-robin, then we'll dive into the packaging and the runtime handoff. Goal is to have a clear path for AtlasPulse to publish the connector into their internal catalog and for us to validate the edge runtime operator in their lab.

[00:18] Ravi K: Yep thanks, excited. We want the minimal friction path — ideally helm chart + image bundle we can sign and push to our private registry. Also need KMS control, and an audit trail for the listing.

[00:34] Liam C: Great. High-level we'll do three deliverables: 1) packaging checklist + canonical helm chart, 2) a short operator-runbook for on-prem edge installs, 3) telemetry + billing hooks for usage metering. I'll go through how our chart is structured and the assumptions.

[00:57] Maya L: Quick note — our security team requires customer-managed KMS and that any keys used for model artifacts are in our KMS namespace. Also our VPC egress is locked down, so the runtime needs to either sit in private subnet with NAT/proxy or run via an approved peering path.

[01:20] Liam C: Understood. The helm chart supports providing external KMS key arns and a secret provider for the node sidecar to mount. We wire through our operator to pass key IDs into the container env, not write them to etcd. There's a caveat around initial bootstrap when downloading model shards — we can either pre-pull images to your registry or stage an S3 presigned path behind your VPC.

[01:48] Ethan B: Sorry can you repeat presigned?

[01:50] Liam C: Sure — presigned S3 URLs or a signed artifact URL used temporarily for the runtime to fetch model artifacts. If you want total network isolation, we can provide an offline bundle (tgz of model + runtime) that you import manually, but that increases operational overhead.

[02:08] Ravi K: Offline bundles are OK for initial pilot, but long term we want managed pull with customer KMS. Also curious about quantization — we have constraints: our edge nodes are T4s and a handful of A10s; cost matters. What's Redwood's recommended quantization profile for latency vs quality?

[02:26] Liam C: For that hardware mix we suggest int8 4-bit (GPTQ-ish) for low-latency inference for short contexts; for long context or higher quality, we recommend int8 hybrid or fp16. We'll include recommended docker variants in the chart values so you can toggle. Note: quantized kernels require a specific operator image that includes fused attention kernels — we'll provide two image tags.

[02:55] Maya L: Are those fused kernels compatible with our K8s runtime? We run a constrained seccomp profile and our admissions controller checks for CAP_SYS_ADMIN blocked.

[03:05] Liam C: We avoid CAP_SYS_ADMIN. The fused kernels are just native libraries, nothing needing extra capabilities. The only thing the operator does is manage device pins and mount the nvidia/cuda drivers. If you run with device plugin, we recommend the device plugin approach rather than privileged containers.

[03:32] Sofia M: Quick commercial callout — for Dedicated customers we have an option for signed bundles and assisted installs; we can include that in the SOW. But today let's focus on the technical handoff.

[03:46] Ravi K: Sounds good. On telemetry: we need per-route token breakdown, latency histograms, and per-model usage billing tags mapped to our internal accounting codes. How does Redwood wire telemetry?

[04:05] Liam C: The runtime emits metrics to Prometheus and traces to Jaeger/OTLP. The helm chart includes a scrape config and optional exporters that can post to your internal telemetry endpoint over HTTPS. For billing tags we support setting route-level metadata that gets emitted with each span/metric; you can map those to your billing system. We'll share a sample PromQL/billing-extraction script.

[04:33] Maya L: Ok good. Make sure we can disable any external calls by toggling env to offline mode.

[04:40] Liam C: Yep — offline mode toggles model fetch and disables auto-update jobs.

[04:49] (short crosstalk)

[04:55] Ethan B: For the catalog metadata itself, what fields are required? We have an internal catalog that needs specific fields: id, version, compatible-hardware, supported-quantization, env-vars, and install-type (operator/standalone).

[05:10] Liam C: We'll provide a sample metadata.json and a small script that validates YAML->metadata. Required fields we suggest: name, id, version, image_tags (for quant profiles), schema_version, recommended_node_selector, network_requirements, security_notes. We'll also add 'canary_strategy' which is how the runtime can route to a fallback model during deploys.

[05:36] Ravi K: On canaries — we want gradual traffic shift and automatic rollback on latency regressions. How adjustable is Redwood's canary?

[05:44] Liam C: It's policy driven — percentage ramp, latency thresholds (p99 and p95), and a fallback to a smaller model variant. The operator integrates with your ingress to shift weight; we can provide an example using Istio or your native k8s service.

[06:05] Maya L: We run an L7 proxy but not Istio. Will that be a problem?

[06:08] Liam C: Not a problem. The helm chart exposes a service and a traffic-mgr sidecar that can do weight-based routing if the proxy supports header-based shards. For more advanced scenarios we can show a sample lua filter for Envoy.

[06:26] Sofia M: Let's capture dependencies: KMS apis, VPC egress info, registry access (for images), telemetry endpoint, and legal/sig contacts for cert.

[06:36] (audio artifact)

[06:40] Ravi K: We'll get those. Also want to surface compliance — SOC2 and audit log retention. Do you provide signed audit logs for operator actions?

[06:50] Liam C: We emit audit logs and can push them to your audit collector. For the hosted offering we keep immutable logs for 90 days by default; for dedicated/private we support configurable retention and export to your SIEM via syslog or forwarder. We'll include a sample retention config.

[07:12] Ethan B: Any blockers we should expect during the lab test?

[07:16] Liam C: Typical blockers: mismatched docker registry credentials, network egress rules blocking presigned S3, and missing GPU driver versions. We'll share a preflight checklist for the lab run. Also one more thing: metrics cardinality — if you enable per-request tags, it can create high cardinality; we recommend sampling or route-level aggregation.

[07:42] Maya L: Noted. On the packaging side, can you sign images so our supply chain folks are happy?

[07:48] Liam C: Yes we support image signing (cosign) and will provide signed manifests. For the offline bundle we can provide a signed tar + checksums.

[07:58] Sofia M: Ok timeline: if we get the VPC info and KMS contact by Apr 1, Liam will push the initial chart PR by Apr 3, then we schedule a lab pair the week of Apr 7 to run the smoke test. That gives engineering time to validate and adjust the chart before you publish to catalog.

[08:18] (background noise)

[08:25] Ravi K: Sounds realistic. One more question — competitor behavior: we've seen OrionEdge force a specific device plugin that required privileged containers. We want to avoid that.

[08:36] Liam C: We avoid privileged containers. We rely on standard device plugins and node-level mounts.

[08:42] Maya L: Ok if you can provide the install steps and runbook we'll take it to sec ops.

[08:48] Liam C: We'll attach a runbook with troubleshooting steps: bootstrap failure modes, keyfetch errors, metric gaps, and guidance on restarting the operator without evicting active pods.

[09:05] Sofia M: Wrap up — recap of owners and dates, and confirm we'll share the GH links after this call.

[09:12] Ravi K: Confirmed. Thanks team.

[09:15] (call ends, informal chat about time zones)

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had some mis-heard technical nouns (e.g., "fused kernels" transcribed as "fuse kernels" in spots) and occasional punctuation drops.
